result:
At three in the morning, the Fourth Street Bridge forgets it is a road and remembers it is a machine.

During the day, commuter traffic presses it into obedience. Tires hum across the steel grating—a rising whine that drifts up into the tender’s house like distant bees—and drivers think of the river only as a brief gap in the asphalt. They don't feel the counterweights. They don't know that directly beneath their axles, sealed inside cavernous concrete pits, hang four hundred tons of cast iron and scrap steel, poised like a held breath.

I know. I spend eight hours a night sitting thirty feet above the roadway, drinking burnt coffee from a dented thermos and listening to the bridge settle its bones.

The tender’s house is an octagonal room wrapped in grime-streaked glass, smelling of ozone, damp wool, and old grease. On the console sit four brass levers, worn smooth by fifty years of palms before mine. Beside them rests the VHF radio, tuned to Channel 13, breathing static into the quiet.

October fog had rolled in from the harbor past midnight, erasing the skyline block by block until only the sodium lamps along the quay remained, glowing like embers in wet ash. Below, black water moved sluggishly toward the bay, carrying a sheen of diesel and the occasional drifting pallet.

I was halfway through a crossword—stuck on a six-letter coastal bird—when the radio coughed.

"Fourth Street, Fourth Street, this is the *Mary K*. Over."

I set my pencil down and keyed the mic. "Fourth Street. Go ahead, *Mary K*."

"Evening, Arthur. Got two barges of crushed limestone pushing upriver. About ten minutes out. Looking for a lift."

"Copy that, *Mary K*. I’ll have her open for you."

The captain’s voice sounded worn soft by diesel thrum and cold air. Most voices on Channel 13 sound like that after two a.m., stripped of daytime hurry. Up here, time doesn’t move in minutes; it moves in knots and currents.

I stood, stretched the stiffness from my back, and watched the approaches. To the east, the street vanished into fog between shuttered warehouses and a bodega whose neon sign flickered blue-white-blue. To the west, a single pair of headlights appeared, crawling through the mist.

I waited until the *Mary K*’s red and green running lights bled around the bend, low and smudged in the vapor. Then I flipped the first switch.

Outside, the warning bells began—a sharp *clank-clank-clank* that always feels impolite in the dead of night, like shouting in a library. Red lights alternated. Slowly, the striped wooden gates descended across both lanes.

The lone car—an old silver hatchback with a rusted fender—rolled to a stop twenty feet shy of the barrier. Its engine idled, sending plumes of white exhaust curling into the red glare. Through the windshield, I made out the silhouette of a driver leaning their forehead against the steering wheel. Not impatient. Just taking the six minutes the river had handed them.

I checked the roadway once more—no stray joggers, no late cyclists ducking the arms—and pulled the tail-lock lever. Deep below the decking, massive steel bolts slid free with a resonant metallic groan.

Then I eased the main control forward.

This is the part nobody gets used to, no matter how long they hold the job. The electric motors whine, climbing in pitch, and the floor beneath your boots shudders. Outside the window, the road breaks in half.

Two hundred feet of steel truss and asphalt tilted skyward, separating at the center seam like a mouth opening. Streetlamps leaned back into the fog at impossible angles. As the two leaves rose to seventy degrees, wind caught the underside of the grating and sang through it, a low hollow chord. For a few minutes, the city was severed—east from west, work from home, one shore from the other.

Below, the *Mary K* slid through the channel. She wasn't much to look at: a squat, pug-nosed tug pushing two flat-decked barges heaped with pale stone. Her wake slapped softly against the pilings. Out on the bow of the lead barge, a deckhand in a yellow slicker stood beside a coiled hawser, watching the clearance. He tilted his head toward my lighted windows and swung his flashlight in a slow arc.

I flicked the overhead cab light off and on twice. *I see you. Safe passage.*

The tug's stern lights drifted past, twin red eyes dissolving back into the gray soup upstream. The wake lapped against the concrete piers, and then even that faded.

I reversed the lever.

Gravity wanted the bridge back; the motors only had to hold its hand on the way down. Slowly, the two great halves descended, closing the wound in the street. I feathered the brake as they neared the horizontal—too fast and you rattle the teeth of every sleeping rat in the abutments; too slow and the center lock binds. They met with a dull, heavy *thump* that traveled up through my soles and settled in my ribs. I drove the locks home, raised the gates, and killed the bells.

Silence rushed back in, thick and damp.

The silver hatchback stayed still for three seconds after the arms lifted. Then the driver sat up, shifted into gear, and rolled onto the grating. Tires resumed their rising hum, carrying whoever it was—a nurse coming off shift, a baker heading in, someone driving just to keep moving—safely across the dark water and into the fog on the other side.

I picked up my pencil and looked down at the crossword. *Dunlin.* Six letters. I printed it carefully into the empty squares, poured the last lukewarm inch of coffee into the plastic lid, and waited for the river to ask again.
